description: How arousal affects sporting performance and the stress management techniques athletes use.
content_html:
What is Arousal?

Arousal is the level of activation or readiness in the mind and body. It sits on a continuous spectrum — from deep sleep at one extreme, through calm alertness, to intense excitement and panic at the other. In sport, arousal is neither simply “nervousness” nor simply “motivation” — it is the physiological and psychological state that underpins how prepared a performer is to act. Heart rate rises, muscles become primed, attention sharpens or narrows. Whether those changes help or hinder performance depends on whether arousal is at the right level for the task.

Two key factors determine the optimal level of arousal for a task: the type of skill involved, and the performer’s experience. A rugby flanker driving into a tackle needs high arousal — the task is physically explosive, relies on gross motor patterns and benefits from heightened aggression. A snooker player lining up a final-frame deciding shot needs low arousal — fine motor control, precision and concentration demand calm. Gross skills tolerate and often benefit from high arousal; fine skills require low arousal to execute precisely.

The Inverted-U Theory

The inverted-U theory describes the relationship between arousal and performance using a characteristic curve. Imagine a graph with arousal level on the x-axis (running left to right from low to high) and performance level on the y-axis (running bottom to top from low to high). The resulting curve rises as arousal increases from zero, reaches a single peak at the point of optimal arousal, then falls symmetrically as arousal continues to climb beyond that peak.

The theory has three zones. In the under-arousal zone (left of the peak), the performer is insufficiently activated: concentration is poor, reactions are slow and motivation is absent. A footballer who is mentally “switched off” before a routine match may misplace simple passes they would never usually get wrong. In the optimal arousal zone (the peak), the performer is precisely prepared — alert, focused and physically primed. In the over-arousal zone (right of the peak), excessive nervousness or excitement floods the system: decision making deteriorates, fine motor control breaks down, and anxiety may cause “choking”. Dina Asher-Smith has spoken candidly about managing the risk of over-arousal before major sprint finals, using controlled breathing and mental routines to stay on the peak rather than tipping over it.

Key Fact

On the inverted-U graph: x-axis = arousal level (low to high), y-axis = performance level (low to high). The peak is ‘optimal arousal’. Left of the peak = under-arousal, performance is low. Right of the peak = over-arousal, performance is also low. The skill type determines where the peak sits: gross skills peak further right (higher arousal needed); fine skills peak further left (lower arousal needed).

Linking Arousal Level to Skill Type

The inverted-U curve does not sit in the same position for every skill. A 100 m sprinter’s optimal arousal point sits towards the higher end of the arousal axis — the explosive, gross motor demands of sprinting are enhanced by a surge in adrenaline, elevated heart rate and heightened muscular tension. But the optimal arousal level for a golfer executing a delicate chip shot from the fringe of a green sits much further left. The precise wrist action, measured swing speed and judged clubface angle all require fine motor control that falls apart under excess activation.

As a rule: gross skills benefit from higher arousal. A tackle in rugby, a power lift in weightlifting, a full-force drive in shot put — all benefit from the extra tension and activation that high arousal brings. Fine skills require lower arousal. Archery, snooker, ten-pin bowling, the free throw in basketball, a conversion kick in rugby — all demand the calm, controlled motor programme execution that high arousal disrupts. This is why a basketball player who is highly aroused may dominate a physical post-up battle but then miss the free throws awarded when they are fouled.

Students often assume the inverted-U peak is in a fixed position for everyone performing the same sport. In reality, the optimal arousal point varies between individuals as well as between skills. A highly experienced athlete who competes regularly at elite level may have a higher optimal arousal threshold — they’ve built the mental skills to channel arousal into performance. A beginner in the same sport may over-arouse much sooner. Additionally, personality influences the threshold: extroverts generally require more stimulation (higher arousal) to reach their optimal point, while introverts can peak at a lower level of activation. The theory is best applied as a guide for the individual performer and the specific skill, not as a universal rule for an entire sport.

Stress Management Techniques

When a performer’s arousal is too high — particularly in high-stakes competition — they need practical tools to bring it back towards optimal. The specification identifies three key techniques: deep breathing, mental rehearsal (visualisation/imagery) and positive self-talk.

Deep breathing works by activating the parasympathetic nervous system, which counteracts the fight-or-flight response of over-arousal. The technique involves inhaling slowly through the nose for a count of four, holding briefly, then exhaling slowly through the mouth for a count of six or eight. The extended exhalation is the physiologically critical part — it drives down heart rate and signals to the brain that the threat level is low. A rugby kicker using deep breathing before a pressure conversion is not wasting time — they are chemically resetting their nervous system. It is used before free throws, set pieces, serves and any moment when a task-specific motor programme must be executed cleanly.

Mental rehearsal — also known as visualisation or imagery — involves the performer building a detailed mental simulation of their performance before it happens. Research shows that vividly imagined movement activates many of the same neural pathways as actually performing it. Adam Peaty has described using detailed visualisation of his 100 m breaststroke race before every major competition, including the sensation of water resistance, the rhythm of his pull, and the moment of turning at the wall. Effective mental rehearsal uses all senses and is always performed in the first person, from the performer’s own perspective, picturing success rather than failure.

Positive self-talk involves consciously replacing negative internal dialogue with pre-planned affirming statements. Athletes under pressure are prone to catastrophic thinking (“I always miss these”, “everyone is watching me fail”). Positive self-talk interrupts this loop: the performer has a prepared phrase — “I have trained for this”, “smooth and accurate”, “trust the process” — that redirects attention onto the task cues rather than the feared outcome. It reduces cognitive anxiety without requiring a physiological reset, making it the quickest of the three techniques to deploy mid-performance.

Key Fact

Three AQA stress management techniques: (1) Deep breathing — slows breathing and heart rate, calms the nervous system, used before or during performance. (2) Mental rehearsal / visualisation / imagery — creates a vivid mental simulation of successful performance, activating the same neural pathways as physical practice. (3) Positive self-talk — replaces negative thoughts with affirming statements to refocus attention and maintain confidence.

Coaches also deal with the opposite problem: athletes who arrive at competition insufficiently aroused, perhaps because the event feels routine or because they are physically fatigued. Under-arousal produces slow reactions, poor concentration, reduced effort and sloppy decision making. Techniques to increase arousal include energetic music, team talks that raise emotional intensity, fast-paced warm-up drills and the coach deliberately raising the perceived stakes of the competition. ‘Psyching up’ strategies are the mirror image of the calming techniques above — the goal is always to land the performer at their personal optimal point on the inverted-U.
exam_tip_html: For a 2 marks — Define question on arousal, you must include both the physical and mental dimension — “a state of physical and mental readiness/activation”. Saying only “being nervous” or “being motivated” earns nothing because it’s too vague. For the inverted-U graph question (“draw and label”), examiners require: a correctly shaped curve, labelled x-axis (arousal level), labelled y-axis (performance level), and the peak labelled ‘optimal arousal’ or equivalent. Unlabelled axes score zero for the labelling marks. On a 9 marks — Evaluate question about arousal and performance, students frequently produce one-sided answers listing only ways arousal helps. Full marks require both the positive effects of optimal arousal and the negative effects of over- or under-arousal, with a sporting example for each point and a balanced conclusion. Structure each paragraph as ‘For… because… for example… However…’ to ensure you cover both sides systematically.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Arousal is the level of physical and mental activation in a performer. The inverted-U theory shows that performance is best at an optimal arousal level — too little causes under-performance through lethargy; too much causes over-performance through anxiety and loss of fine motor control.
  • Optimal arousal varies by skill type: gross skills (tackling, sprinting, throwing) require higher arousal; fine skills (archery, snooker, a penalty kick) require lower arousal to preserve motor precision.
  • Three stress management techniques lower over-arousal: deep breathing (slows heart rate via the parasympathetic system), mental rehearsal/visualisation (simulates successful performance), and positive self-talk (replaces negative thoughts with affirming cues).

practice_questions.text: Identify the term used to describe the arousal level at which performance is at its highest on the inverted-U graph.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for 'optimal arousal' or equivalent (e.g. 'optimum arousal', 'peak arousal point').

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'arousal' in the context of sporting performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a physical dimension of arousal (e.g. increased heart rate, heightened muscle tension, physical readiness); 1 mark for identifying a mental/psychological dimension (e.g. alertness, mental readiness, state of activation). A definition that addresses only one dimension earns 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the inverted-U theory explains what happens to performance when a competitor is over-aroused.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that arousal has risen beyond the optimal point on the curve; 1 mark for describing the effect on performance (performance decreases / deteriorates / drops from its peak); 1 mark for identifying a mechanism or example (e.g. fine motor control breaks down, decision making deteriorates, anxiety increases, choking occurs under pressure — or a specific sport example such as a tennis player double-faulting due to excess nerves).

practice_questions.text: A club-level archer is preparing for a county championship and tells her coach she feels 'absolutely terrified'. Explain how mental rehearsal could help her manage her arousal before she shoots.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that mental rehearsal / visualisation / imagery is a stress management technique; 1 mark for explaining what it involves (creating a detailed internal image of successfully executing the skill, using all senses, first-person perspective); 1 mark for linking to arousal reduction (activating the same neural pathways as physical practice, building confidence, reducing cognitive anxiety); 1 mark for specific application to the archery context (e.g. she visualises drawing the bow, holding, releasing and the arrow striking the gold, building the feeling that she has 'been here before').

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old county-level sprinter competes well in training but consistently underperforms in major competitions. Her coach believes she becomes over-aroused on race day. Analyse the stress management techniques available to the sprinter and how each could help her return to optimal arousal.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses all three techniques (deep breathing, mental rehearsal, positive self-talk) with a clear explanation of how each works physiologically or psychologically, and specific application to the sprinter's situation. Evaluates which technique(s) suit the timing of arousal management (pre-race vs on-the-blocks). Recognises that sprinting is a gross skill and therefore the optimal arousal point is higher than for a fine skill, meaning only modest reduction is needed.

Secure: Covers at least two techniques with explanation of mechanism and sporting application. May not evaluate timing or skill-type suitability. Some analysis rather than pure description.

Developing: Names two or more techniques and briefly explains one. Limited application to the sprinter specifically. Mostly descriptive.

Emerging: Names one technique with limited explanation. No sporting application.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the view that the inverted-U theory fully explains the relationship between arousal and performance in sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Presents a balanced evaluation with well-developed points on both sides. Arguments in support: the theory correctly predicts that both under- and over-arousal reduce performance; it accounts for skill-type variation (gross vs fine); it provides coaches with a practical framework for monitoring and adjusting arousal. Arguments against or limitations: the theory assumes a single smooth peak for all tasks and all athletes, but individual differences (personality type — introvert vs extrovert, experience level) mean the curve shifts position; the theory does not explain why some athletes 'choke' catastrophically rather than declining gradually. Reaches a justified conclusion. Uses sporting examples throughout.

Secure: Presents both sides with some development. At least one limitation identified. Sporting examples present. May not fully balance both sides or justify the conclusion.

Developing: Mostly one-sided (either supporting or criticising the theory). Some relevant points but limited development. Sporting application may be absent.

Emerging: Basic points only, largely descriptive. No meaningful balance.

knowledge_checks.q: On the inverted-U graph, what happens to performance when arousal rises beyond the optimal point?
options: Performance stays at its peak level

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of skill requires the lowest optimal arousal level for best performance?
Deep breathing helps reduce over-arousal by slowing the heart rate and activating the _____ nervous system.
Mental rehearsal is also known as _____ or imagery, and involves creating a vivid internal image of successful performance.
Match each stress management technique to how it works:
right: Slows heart rate by activating the parasympathetic nervous system
Replaces negative thoughts with prepared affirming statements
Creates a vivid mental simulation of successful performance

flashcard_questions.a: A state of physical and mental activation or readiness, from deep sleep to extreme excitement.

flashcard_questions.q: What shape does the inverted-U theory produce on a graph?
flashcard_questions.a: An inverted U — performance rises with arousal to a peak, then falls as arousal increases further.

flashcard_questions.q: What label goes on the x-axis of the inverted-U graph?
What label goes on the y-axis of the inverted-U graph?

flashcard_questions.a: The arousal level at which performance is at its highest point on the inverted-U curve.

flashcard_questions.q: Do gross skills require higher or lower optimal arousal than fine skills?
flashcard_questions.a: Higher — gross skills like tackling benefit from increased muscle tension and activation.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of a fine skill that requires low arousal for best performance.
flashcard_questions.a: An archery shot, a snooker pot, or a free throw in basketball.

flashcard_questions.q: How does deep breathing reduce over-arousal?
flashcard_questions.a: Slow exhalation activates the parasympathetic nervous system, lowering heart rate.

flashcard_questions.q: What is mental rehearsal in sport?
flashcard_questions.a: A vivid internal mental simulation of successfully performing a skill, using all senses.
Replacing negative thoughts with prepared affirming statements to refocus attention.

flashcard_questions.q: What effect does under-arousal have on performance?
flashcard_questions.a: Performance is low — reactions are slow, concentration is poor, effort is reduced.

flashcard_questions.q: Which personality type typically requires higher arousal to reach their optimal performance point?
flashcard_questions.a: Extroverts — they need more stimulation to reach optimal activation.

glossary_terms.definition: A state of physical and mental readiness or activation, ranging from deep sleep to extreme excitement, that affects how a performer responds in a sporting situation.
A theory proposing that performance increases as arousal rises to an optimal point, then decreases as arousal continues to increase beyond that point, producing an inverted-U shape on a graph.

A controlled breathing technique in which a performer deliberately slows and deepens their breathing to lower heart rate, reduce muscle tension and calm the nervous system before or during competition.
A mental technique in which a performer creates a detailed internal image of themselves successfully executing a skill or performance, engaging all senses to make the rehearsal as vivid as possible.
A technique in which a performer deliberately replaces negative thoughts with prepared, affirming statements to maintain focus and confidence under pressure.
A state in which arousal rises beyond the optimal point, causing anxiety, loss of concentration and a decline in sporting performance.

items.title: Don't Tell Me the Score — Jonny Wilkinson: Managing Anxiety and Arousal
items.description: Wilkinson's famously detailed pre-kick routines and anxiety management techniques are a real-world application of arousal control strategies and the inverted-U theory.

items.title: High Performance Podcast — Dina Asher-Smith on Racing Under Pressure
items.description: Jake Humphrey and Damian Hughes discuss how Asher-Smith manages pre-race arousal, uses mental rehearsal and stays at her optimal arousal level before sprint finals.

items.title: How Stress Affects Your Body — TED-Ed
items.description: Explains the physiological mechanisms of the stress response — the same systems that drive arousal — helping students understand why over-arousal impairs fine motor performance.

items.title: Flow, the Secret to Happiness — Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi | TED
items.description: Csikszentmihalyi's theory of peak performance states parallels the inverted-U concept: optimal arousal is the entry point to flow, where performance peaks.

items.title: The Happy Secret to Better Work — Shawn Achor | TED
items.description: Achor's positive psychology research explains why optimal rather than maximal arousal improves performance and decision making in high-pressure situations.

items.title: Free Solo (2018)
items.description: Alex Honnold's mastery of arousal control under potentially fatal pressure is a documentary study of optimal arousal for a gross-motor, high-stakes skill.

items.title: Senna (2010)
items.description: Ayrton Senna's pre-race mental routines and his accounts of driving in a state beyond conscious control illustrate the inverted-U peak — and what lies beyond it.

items.title: BBC Bitesize — Arousal and the Inverted-U Theory
items.description: AQA-aligned notes on the inverted-U graph, optimal arousal, stress management techniques and how arousal varies with skill type.

items.title: tutor2u — Inverted-U Theory Revision Notes
items.description: GCSE PE revision covering the arousal-performance relationship, the three zones of the inverted-U curve, and deep breathing, visualisation and self-talk techniques.
